sections.title: Lesson 11.1: Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and the Bank Secrecy Act
sections.overview: Money laundering is the process of disguising illicit funds as legitimate income; post-9/11 AML rules also target the use of clean money for illicit purposes (e.g., terrorist financing). The Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), administered through the U.S. Treasury and enforced via FinCEN, requires broker-dealers to maintain AML compliance programs, file currency and suspicious activity reports, and screen customers against OFAC's SDN list.
key_concepts: Three stages of money laundering: (1) Placement — introducing illicit cash into the financial system (most detectable stage); (2) Layering — series of transactions designed to obscure the origin; (3) Integration — funds re-enter the economy appearing legitimate.
FinCEN — bureau of U.S. Treasury (not DOJ); intelligence agency with no direct enforcement arm; receives CTRs and SARs.

Currency Transaction Report (CTR): required for cash transactions > $10,000 in a single day (single or aggregated). Filed within 15 days. Records kept 5 years. Applies to currency only — not checks or wires; not limited to U.S. dollars.
Structuring: designing cash deposits/withdrawals to fall below the $10,000 CTR threshold — itself a prohibited act.

Suspicious Activity Report (SAR): required for transactions ≥ $5,000 that appear to involve illicit funds, evade BSA, lack business purpose, or facilitate criminal activity. Filed within 30 days (60 if no suspect identified). SARs are confidential — subject must NOT be notified.
USA PATRIOT Act: also requires record retention on wire transfers ≥ $3,000 (names, addresses, amount, financial institution, recipient account).

AML Compliance Program (Rule 3310) — five required elements: (1) written policies/procedures, (2) designated AML compliance officer (need not be registered), (3) ongoing training, (4) independent annual testing, (5) customer identification program (CIP).

Customer Identification Program (CIP): collect name, DOB, address, and ID number (e.g., SSN/TIN) before opening account; verify identity; notify customer that information is being requested for identification.

OFAC — division of U.S. Treasury — publishes the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list; U.S. persons (including BDs and RRs) are prohibited from doing business with anyone on the list; assets of SDNs must be blocked.

AML red flags: customer indifferent to risk/cost; frequent or large currency deposits; many wires to unrelated third parties; excessive journal entries between unrelated accounts; apparent structuring.
rules: Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) — Treasury rulemaking authority for AML.
USA PATRIOT Act (2001) — expanded AML rules, mandated CIP and SAR filings.
FINRA Rule 3310 — AML Compliance Program (5 required elements).
CTR filing: > $10,000 cash in a day; file within 15 days; retain records 5 years; max penalty $500,000 / 10 years / both.
SAR filing: ≥ $5,000 if suspicious; file within 30 days; retain 5 years; strict confidentiality.
formulas: CTR trigger: aggregate same-day currency in/out > $10,000
mnemonics: Stages of laundering: 'PLI' — Placement, Layering, Integration.
AML program 5 pillars: 'PACTI' — Policies, AML officer, CIP, Training, Independent testing.
CTR = Cash, Ten thousand, Reports (15 days). SAR = Suspicious, About 5 (thousand), 30 days.

sections.title: Lesson 11.2: Market Manipulation and Insider Trading
sections.overview: No security is exempt from antifraud provisions. Market manipulation includes any conduct intended to deceive market participants or distort the natural pricing of securities. Insider trading — trading on or tipping material nonpublic information (MNPI) — carries severe civil and criminal penalties under the Insider Trading and Securities Fraud Enforcement Act of 1988 (ITSFEA).
key_concepts: Market rumors — spreading false or misleading information (including via social media) to move prices is prohibited.
Pump and dump — accumulate shares, inflate price with false positive rumors, then sell into the buying frenzy.
Front running — placing a personal order ahead of a known pending block order to profit from the expected price movement.
Churning (excessive trading) — trading to generate commissions rather than meet client objectives; violates fiduciary duty; principals must review accounts, especially discretionary ones.
Marking the open / marking the close — entering or falsely reporting trades at/near the open or close to manipulate the reported opening/closing price.
Freeriding — buying then selling before paying; account frozen 90 days.
Matching orders / painting the tape — coordinated buy/sell between parties to create the illusion of volume.
Insider trading: trading on (or tipping) material nonpublic information. Possession of MNPI is not illegal; using it to gain or avoid loss is.
Material info = info that would reasonably affect a stock's price. Nonpublic = not disseminated to the general public.

Tipper/tippee liability four-part test: (1) info material and nonpublic; (2) tipper owes fiduciary duty; (3) tipper benefits (personal benefit test); (4) tippee knew or should have known info was improper.
Contemporaneous traders — traders opposite an insider may sue for up to 5 years after the violation.
Bounties (Dodd-Frank): informants may receive 10%–30% of amounts recovered.
Firewall / information barrier — written procedures restricting MNPI flow between firm departments.

Rule 5130 — restricted persons may NOT purchase new equity IPOs at the POP. Includes member firms, their employees, finders/fiduciaries to the underwriter, portfolio managers, owners of 10%+ of a member, and their immediate family.

Immediate family under 5130: parents, in-laws, spouse, siblings, children, and anyone the person materially supports. Aunts/uncles/grandparents are NOT immediate family unless living in the same household or materially supported.
De minimis exemption (5130): an account can buy IPOs if restricted persons' beneficial interest does not exceed 10% of the account.
Rule 5131 — prohibits 'spinning' (allocating IPOs to executives/directors of companies in a position to direct future investment-banking business).
rules: Securities Exchange Act of 1934 §10(b) and Rule 10b-5 — antifraud, manipulation, and insider-trading prohibitions.

Insider Trading & Securities Fraud Enforcement Act of 1988 (ITSFEA) — civil penalty up to 3x profit gained/loss avoided; criminal up to $5,000,000 and 20 years for individuals; firm penalty up to greater of $25 million or 3x damages; controlling person up to greater of $1 million or 3x.
FINRA Rule 5130 — restrictions on IPO purchases.
FINRA Rule 5131 — anti-spinning and new-issue allocation abuses.
FINRA Rules 5270 (front running of block transactions), 5280 (trading ahead of research reports), 5320 (trading ahead of customer orders).
formulas: Civil insider-trading penalty (individual) = up to 3 × (profit gained or loss avoided)
Criminal insider-trading max (individual) = $5,000,000 fine and/or 20 years imprisonment
Firm penalty for failure to supervise = greater of $25,000,000 or 3 × damages
Dodd-Frank bounty range = 10%–30% of amount recovered
mnemonics: Manipulation acts: 'FRMP-MC' — Front-running, Rumors, Matching orders, Pump-and-dump, Marking Close/open, Churning.
Tipper/tippee test: 'MNFB' — Material/Nonpublic, Fiduciary breach, Benefit to tipper, Knowledge by tippee.
5130 restricted family — 'PISCS' (Parents, In-laws, Spouse, Children, Siblings); aunts/uncles/grandparents OUT.

sections.title: Lesson 11.3: Prohibited Activities — Senior Clients, Customer Assets, and Unregistered Personnel
sections.overview: Beyond market manipulation, FINRA prohibits a range of activities that exploit customer relationships or misuse customer assets. Special protections apply to 'specified adults' (seniors and the mentally/physically impaired) under Rule 2165, and strict limits govern borrowing, lending, guarantees, sharing in accounts, and the activities of nonregistered personnel.
key_concepts: Specified adult: (a) age 65 or older, or (b) age 18 or older whom the firm reasonably believes has a mental or physical impairment that renders them unable to protect their own interests.

Trusted contact person (Rule 4512): firms must make reasonable efforts to obtain name and contact at account opening or when updating. Account may still be opened if the customer refuses, provided reasonable effort was made.

Temporary holds (Rule 2165): firm MAY (not must) place a temporary hold on disbursements OR securities transactions if it reasonably believes financial exploitation has occurred/is occurring/is being attempted.

Hold durations under amended Rule 2165 (effective 3/17/2022): initial hold up to 15 business days; firm may internally extend by up to 10 additional business days (25 total); if reported to a state regulator/agency/court, additional 30-business-day extension (up to 55 business days total).

Firm must initiate an internal review immediately and notify the trusted contact person and other authorized parties within 2 business days — unless the trusted contact is suspected of perpetrating the exploitation or is unavailable.

Improper use of customer assets: any use of customer funds/securities other than as intended is prohibited. Red flags: suspicious transfers, activity in deceased persons' accounts, excessive complaints, address/phone inconsistencies.

Borrowing/lending with customers (Rule 3240): firm must have written procedures permitting it; written prior notice and (usually) firm approval required. Five permitted categories: (1) immediate family (no notice/approval); (2) customer in the business of lending, e.g., a bank (no approval); (3) both are registered with same firm (approval); (4) personal relationship outside the broker-customer relationship (approval); (5) business relationship outside the broker-customer relationship (approval).
Guarantees prohibited — BDs/IAs/RRs may not guarantee a customer against loss or guarantee a gain.

Sharing in customer accounts (Rule 2150): only with prior written firm approval and only in direct proportion to financial contribution. Exception: directly proportionate sharing not required for immediate family joint accounts. Firms cannot have joint accounts with customers.

Rule 3241 (effective 2/15/2021): registered person being named as a customer's beneficiary, executor, trustee, or holder of power of attorney for a non-immediate-family customer requires written notice to and written approval by the firm.

Nonregistered personnel may: respond to general administrative questions, send literature on request, schedule appointments, invite to seminars; may handle customer money/securities (must be fingerprinted).
Nonregistered personnel may NOT: solicit trades, open accounts, accept orders, give recommendations, or otherwise engage in the securities business.
Passing the SIE alone does NOT register you — you must also pass a top-off (representative-level) exam.
rules: FINRA Rule 2165 — Financial Exploitation of Specified Adults; holds on disbursements and securities transactions; 15 + 10 + 30 business-day structure (max 55 b.d.).
FINRA Rule 4512 — customer account information, including trusted contact.
FINRA Rule 2150 — improper use; prohibition against guarantees and sharing in accounts.
FINRA Rule 3240 — borrowing from or lending to customers.
FINRA Rule 3241 — registered person being named beneficiary or fiduciary; firm notice/approval required.
FINRA Rule 2040 — payments to unregistered persons prohibited.
formulas: Rule 2165 maximum hold timeline = 15 b.d. (initial) + 10 b.d. (internal extension) + 30 b.d. (regulator/court extension) = 55 business days total
mnemonics: 3240 lending OK list: 'IB-RPB' — Immediate family, Bank-type customer, Registered same-firm, Personal outside relationship, Business outside relationship.
Nonregistered can: 'Greet, schedule, hand-out — never solicit.'

sections.title: Lesson 11.4: Communications with the Public, Telemarketing, Statements, Regulation S-P, and BCP
sections.overview: FINRA Rule 2210 classifies all member communications into three categories — institutional, retail, and correspondence — each with its own filing, approval, and recordkeeping requirements. The TCPA governs cold-calling; firms must also satisfy account-statement and confirmation delivery, hold-mail rules, Regulation S-P privacy obligations (including new 2024 incident-response amendments), and maintain a business continuity plan.
key_concepts: All communications must be fair and balanced, based on principles of good faith, not misleading, not omit material facts, never imply that past performance will be repeated, and consider the nature of the audience.

Institutional communication: written/electronic communication distributed only to institutional investors. Institutional investors include other BDs/RRs, banks, S&Ls, insurance companies, registered investment companies, employee benefit plans, governmental entities, and any entity (including a natural person) with ≥ $50 million in total assets. Cannot be treated as institutional if firm has reason to believe it will be forwarded to retail.

Retail communication: written/electronic communication distributed/made available to MORE THAN 25 retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period. Requires principal approval before use; must be filed with FINRA.
Filing timing: new member firms (first year) — file at least 10 days BEFORE use; established firms — file within 10 days OF first use. Filing is not approval.

Correspondence: written/electronic to 25 or fewer retail investors within 30 calendar days. Firm sets policy on pre- or post-use principal review; if post-use, firm must provide training and documentation.
Social media: static content (websites, profiles, blogs) typically requires principal pre-approval; interactive posts do not require pre-approval but must be supervised under written procedures.

Telephone Consumer Protection Act of 1991 (TCPA): cold calls only between 8:00 am and 9:00 pm at the called party's local time; caller must identify name, firm, and firm phone/address; firm must maintain a do-not-call list and screen against the National DNC Registry (lists must be ≤ 30 days old).
TCPA exemptions: calls to parties with established business relationship or prior express consent; calls on behalf of tax-exempt nonprofits; non-commercial calls; legitimate debt collection.
Account statements: at least quarterly; monthly if there is activity in the account or penny stocks are held. Must disclose to the customer to promptly report any inaccuracy.
Free credit balances: may be held by firm but statement must disclose funds are available on request.

Trade confirmations (SEC Rule 10b-10 / FINRA 2232): delivered at or before completion (settlement). Includes trade date, account number, RR ID, buy/sell, quantity, security, yield (if applicable), CUSIP, price, principal amount, commission (agency) or capacity disclosure (principal markup/markdown), net amount, and capacity (agent vs. principal).

Holding customer mail (Rule 3150): firm may hold mail with written customer instructions, normally for up to 3 months (longer for safety/security reasons but not mere convenience); firm must provide alternative access (e.g., online), verify the instruction periodically, and be able to reach the customer for important information.
Account record verification (Rule 4512): firm must send copy of account record to customer within 30 days of opening, within 30 days of any change, and at least every 36 months thereafter.

Regulation S-P: protects nonpublic personal information (e.g., SSN, balances, transaction history). Initial privacy notice at the start of the customer relationship and annually thereafter. Customers must be given a reasonable opt-out method for sharing with nonaffiliated third parties (check-off form with prepaid envelope, electronic opt-out, or toll-free number — writing a letter is NOT a reasonable method).
Reg S-P safeguard rule: protect customer info across all forms of existing/developing technology (secure devices, encrypt email, etc.).

Reg S-P (amended 5/15/2024): firms must adopt a written incident-response program; provide customer notification within 30 days of unauthorized access to or use of sensitive customer information; expanded vendor-oversight requirements. Large-entity compliance date 12/3/2025; small-entity 6/3/2026.
Consumers vs. customers: a consumer has a one-time/limited interaction (initial notice only); a customer has an ongoing relationship (initial + annual).

Business Continuity Plan (Rule 4370): written plan addressing data backup/recovery, alternate communications with customers/employees, alternate physical location, communications with regulators, and prompt customer access to funds/securities. Must be reviewed annually by a designated senior principal.

Emergency contacts: firm must provide FINRA with two emergency contact persons (both associated persons; at least one a member of senior management who is also a principal; if a single-person firm, may use a non-associated person familiar with operations). Updates required promptly, no later than 30 days after any change.
BCP disclosure: must be given to customers at account opening, posted on website, and mailed on request.
rules: FINRA Rule 2210 — Communications with the Public (institutional / retail / correspondence).
FINRA Rule 2232 — Customer Confirmations; SEC Rule 10b-10.
FINRA Rule 2231 — Customer Account Statements.
FINRA Rule 3150 — Holding of Customer Mail.
FINRA Rule 3230 — Telemarketing; TCPA of 1991 (FCC).
FINRA Rule 4370 — Business Continuity Plans and Emergency Contact Information.
FINRA Rule 4512 — Customer Account Information (including 30/30/36-month updates).
SEC Regulation S-P — Privacy of Consumer Financial Information; Safeguard Rule; 2024 amendments add incident response and 30-day customer notification.
formulas: Retail communication threshold: > 25 retail investors / 30 calendar days
Correspondence threshold: ≤ 25 retail investors / 30 calendar days
Filing window — new member: ≥ 10 days BEFORE first use; established member: within 10 days AFTER first use
Calling hours under TCPA: 8:00 am – 9:00 pm at called party's local time
Account record refresh: within 30 days of opening / 30 days of change / at least every 36 months
Reg S-P breach notification (2024 amendment): within 30 days of unauthorized access/use
mnemonics: Retail = '25 in 30' rule (more than 25 retail in any 30 days).
TCPA: 'Call 8-to-9, in their time zone, off the no-call line.'
Reg S-P timing: 'Initial, Annual, and (now) 30-day incident.'
BCP contacts: 'Two persons, one principal, senior.'
